To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the brain is a hierarchical, modular network with rich functionality emerging from its invariant structural architecture, and that this rich functionality is achieved by a degenerate (manyto-one) function- structure mapping.

(i) brain networks are modular and hierarchically organized, (ii) functional networks are context-sensitive and dynamic, (iii) the function-structure mapping of the brain is degenerate and non-trivial, and (iv) a formal approach to neuronal information integration is required to understand how the brain works.

the brain's structural architecture is highly conserved across mammalian species, and that this invariant structural architecture is a key determinant of the rich functional diversity of brain activity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) What is the structural architecture of brain networks?
understanding the structural and functional architecture of brain networks and how this architecture constrains the emergence of cognition.
the structural and functional organization of the human brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the structural architecture of the connectome constrains the functional organization of the connectome, but does not determine it.
the structural and functional brain network architectures are complementary and that their interplay is crucial for understanding cognition.
the structural architecture of the human brain is highly modular and hierarchically organized, but that the brain's function is highly dynamic and context-sensitive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain is a complex system with hierarchical organization, which is characterized by the coexistence of segregated and integrated neuronal operations.
the brain's structural architecture is invariant, but its functional architecture is context-sensitive, which is the basis for the brain's rich functionality.
the structural architecture of the cortex is a hierarchical modular network, which supports rich and flexible cognitive functions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
network theory can provide new insights into the nature of the brain as a complex network system, and that these insights may be used for developing novel computational models for brain networks.

the structural network architecture of the human brain may be more constrained than previously thought, but that this architecture is nevertheless flexible enough to support the diverse and complex cognitive processes we experience every day.
the rich repertoire of neuronal computations is not only enabled by the rich structural connectivity but also constrained by it.
